description: On the five-list build of `main` at `43403ac` (run 20261019T0759116033000000) the 51 ion substances published under six spellings: IUPAC charge numbers (`Lead(2+)`), the American element with a charge number (`Cesium(1+)`), a Roman numeral (`Chromium IV`), the bare anion (`Chloride`), and the generic ion as `Copper, Ion` and as `Titanium, ion`. The spellings inventories use were synonyms only by accident: ecoinvent 3.12's `Lead II` was not one of lead(2+)'s, and `Chromium, Ion` had no synonyms at all. #401 is the standard, in `domain/ion_names.py`: a cation is `Lead(2+)` and answers to `Lead(II)` and `Lead II`; an anion is `Chloride(1-)` and answers to `Chloride`, `Chloride(-I)` and `Chloride -I`; an ion of unstated charge is `Copper, ion` and answers to `Copper, Ion` and `Copper Ion`; the element is spelled as IUPAC spells it, and every form is repeated in the American spelling where that differs. `pipeline/ion_names.py` applies it last of the substance-name writers, and to the substances the merge mints. Selected by substance id where the label is what changes, because a label selector would find nothing on one side. `label` and `alt_label` compare without regard to case, so a respelling that only lowers `Ion` to `ion` is claimed through its synonyms.

expectations.title: ecoinvent's `Lead II` is a synonym of `Lead(2+)`
expectations.comment: The example the issue opens with. On the build of `43403ac` lead(2+) carried `Lead (ii)` and `lead(II) ion` but not ecoinvent 3.12's own `Lead II`.

expectations.title: Caesium(1+) is published in IUPAC's spelling and answers to the American one
expectations.comment: `Cesium(1+)` on the build of `43403ac`, the one charged ion in the American spelling. The element itself stays `Cesium`: the standard is about ions.

expectations.title: Chloride is published as `Chloride(1-)` and answers to `Chloride` and `Chloride -I`
expectations.comment: One of the five monatomic anions, published as the bare anion name on the build of `43403ac`. The charge is read off the substance, because the bare name states it by being an anion's.

expectations.title: Sulfide is published as `Sulfide(2-)`
expectations.comment: The anion with two charges, so the numeral is `-II`.

expectations.title: `Chromium IV` is published as `Chromium(4+)`, though it is typed a mixture
expectations.comment: Typed `ImpreciseChemicalMixture` on the build of `43403ac` (#628), and recorded as the ion of chromium with a stated charge of 4: read as an ion by that record, which only an element's name can produce.

expectations.title: `Chromium, ion` answers to `Chromium, Ion` and `Chromium Ion`
expectations.comment: Minted by the merge from a vendor's `X, ion`, title-cased as `Chromium, Ion` and published with no synonyms on the build of `43403ac`.

expectations.title: `Copper, ion` keeps `Copper, Ion` as a synonym
expectations.comment: Published as `Copper, Ion` on the build of `43403ac`, with only `Copper Ion` beside it. The standard spells the label `Copper, ion` and publishes both capitalised spellings.

expectations.title: `Titanium, ion` keeps its unstated charge and gains its capitalised spellings
expectations.comment: The leave-alone half. PubChem gives the payload Ti+4, and #143 ruled that the name still says no charge; the standard spells names and does not decide charges, so the label is unchanged and only the synonyms are new.

expectations.title: `Methylmercury(1+)` gains no Roman-numeral synonym
expectations.comment: The other leave-alone half. A numeral states an oxidation number, which is the charge only for one atom: methylmercury's mercury is mercury(II), so `Methylmercury(I)` would be wrong. Nothing about it is ion-standard business, which this claims by its label and type standing.
